revulsion

rih-VUL-shun · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Revulsion is a strong feeling of disgust.

The jury's faces showed open revulsion as the prosecutor described the crime scene in detail.

Worked Example

Watching the documentary about the polluted river, viewers reported feeling genuine revulsion at the sight of dead fish floating for miles downstream.

Revulsion is more than dislike -- it's a strong, almost physical reaction of disgust.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disgust: Disgust is the broad, everyday word for the sick, repelled feeling that something foul stirs up, at any strength. Revulsion is disgust at full force -- a reaction so strong it feels almost physical, making you flinch or turn away. Litter earns disgust; cruelty earns revulsion.

repulsion: Repulsion is the sense of being actively pushed away, as if the vile thing itself were driving you back a step. Revulsion points inward instead: the churning, almost bodily disgust rising in your own stomach. Repulsion is the push you feel from the thing; revulsion is the sickness inside you.

loathing: Loathing is hatred that has settled in over time -- you loathe what you know well and despise deeply. Revulsion is sudden: a wave of almost physical disgust that hits the moment you see or learn of something vile, even something you never hated before.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

attraction: a strong feeling of being drawn toward something

delight: a feeling of great pleasure

Where it sits · how intense the dislike becomes — distaste → revulsion → horror

distaste vs. revulsion: Distaste is only a faint wrinkle of the nose -- a mild dislike sitting far below revulsion, which turns the stomach.

horror vs. revulsion: Horror goes a step beyond revulsion by adding fear: revulsion sickens you, while horror sickens and frightens you at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back, away (Latin)

root — vuls-

root — vuls-: to pull, to tear (from Latin vellere, whose past stem is vuls-)

suffix — -ion

suffix — -ion: the act or state of; forms a noun (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Revulsion is built from re- ('back, away') + vuls- ('to pull, to tear,' from Latin vellere, whose past stem is vuls-) + -ion (a noun ending) -- literally a sudden 'pulling back' or 'tearing away,' which captures exactly how your body reacts when something disgusts you.

Use the root in a new word: convulsion

Use the root in a new word: convulsion: The patient's muscles shook with a brief convulsion before the medication finally took effect.
